name: Lemon & sweet chili chicken (עוף בלימון וצ'ילי מתוק)

source.author: Instagram (Hebrew caption)
source.notes: A Korean-style double-fried chicken: pieces marinated in soy/garlic/pepper, coated in a settled-potato-starch-and-egg batter (the 'let the starch settle, pour off the clear water' technique), fried twice for crunch, then tossed in a sweet-chili-honey-soy-lemon sauce. The post itself flags that sweet chili brands vary — taste and adjust the honey to match. Analyzed with ~700 g raw chicken breast (10-12 pieces) and ~90 g of oil assumed absorbed across the double-fry (a meaningful amount, typical for twice-fried battered chicken). This is the heaviest-sauce, most indulgent recipe of this batch — closer to a treat/occasional dish than a regular rotation candidate. Estimate.

serving_desc: ≈320 g cooked (batch ÷4) — chicken + sauce, not including rice

ingredients.note: sweetness varies a lot by brand — taste before adding all the honey

steps: Mix the chicken pieces with the soy sauce, crushed garlic and black pepper.
Combine the starch and water 1:1 and let it sit 15–20 min until the starch settles; carefully pour off the clear water on top.
Stir the egg and oil into the settled starch; thin with a little more water if the mixture is too thick.
Coat the chicken pieces in the starch batter and fry in hot oil; remove, then fry a second time until deep golden and crispy.
In a small pot, combine the sweet chili sauce, honey, soy sauce and water; simmer gently, stirring, until it thickens slightly.
Add the lemon slices and the fried chicken; toss over low heat for about 30 seconds to a minute, just until coated — don't overcook, to keep the coating crispy.

batch_totals.note: Whole dish (4 servings), excl. rice. The double-fry plus a very large sweet-chili-and-honey sauce (12 tbsp of sweetener combined) make this by far the most calorie- and sugar-dense dish added this round — closer to a restaurant-style treat than an everyday meal.

him.verdict: Tasty, but this is clearly an occasional treat, not a cut-friendly staple. ~40.5 g protein is solid in absolute terms, but it comes with ~754 kcal, ~75 g carbs and ~41 g of added sugar per serving (~5.4 g protein per 100 kcal — the lowest protein density of anything added this round). The double-fried starch coating plus 8 tbsp sweet chili + 4 tbsp honey is a lot of sugar and starch stacked together. Nothing wrong with making it occasionally, but it doesn't fit a daily rotation the way the library's other chicken dishes do.
flags: ~40.5 g protein but ~754 kcal/serving (~5.4 g protein per 100 kcal — low density for this library)
~41 g added sugar/serving — sweet chili sauce + honey, a lot of sweetener
the single sweetest, most calorie-dense dish of this batch
suggested_mods: Treat this as an occasional dish, not a regular rotation meal
Halve the sauce (4 tbsp sweet chili + 2 tbsp honey) — still plenty of glaze, meaningfully less sugar
Single-fry instead of double-fry if you want less oil, accepting a slightly less crunchy result
Serve with a big side salad to add fiber and bulk the meal out without adding calories

her_preconception.verdict: Fully cooked chicken, no safety flags. But this is a high-sugar, high-fat, low-fiber dish with essentially nothing to offer her preconception priorities (no meaningful folate, iron, choline or omega-3) — it's a treat, same read as for him. Fine occasionally; not a dish to build a regular rotation around.
prenatal_highlights: protein from the chicken; fully cooked
suggested_mods: Keep this occasional rather than routine
Pair with a vegetable side for any folate/fiber, which the dish itself doesn't provide

cooking_guide: Let the starch-and-water mixture settle the full 15–20 min — rushing this step means you pour off starch along with the water instead of just the clear liquid on top.
Pour off the clear water SLOWLY and carefully, tilting the bowl gently — the wet starch paste at the bottom is what you want to keep.
The double-fry is the real crunch secret: the first fry cooks the chicken through at a lower temperature, the second fry (hotter, shorter) is purely for color and crispness. Don't skip either step.
Fry in batches so the oil temperature doesn't drop — crowded pieces steam each other and the coating turns soft instead of crisp.
Taste the sauce before adding all the honey — sweet chili brands vary a lot in sweetness, as the original recipe itself notes, so build it up rather than dumping it all in.
Toss the fried chicken in the sauce for only 30 seconds to a minute, off or over very low heat — any longer and the crispy coating starts to soften in the liquid.
Tip: for a lighter version, cut the sauce roughly in half and single-fry instead of double-frying — you'll lose a little crunch but keep real flavor with much less sugar and oil.
